title: Black audiences for jazz in Philadelphia
summary: Waters agrees that the Philadelphia jazz bands and their road gigs played mostly for Black audiences, who appreciated the music first, while his brother played rich people's parlors.

story.theme_name: Race and segregation in the jazz life
story.community_name: Segregation on the road and the bandstand

blocks.x: Yeah, but you said that was, that was primarily for black dancing.
How about the ballroom you were playing with -
It was for a black audience -
Were you playing for a, for strictly black audiences in the Philadelphia area?
Not with my brother, my brother, he played with rich people's parlors and things, he has a, you now, big difference there.
Right, but would the jazz orchestras, the jazz -
But the gigging, like on the Eastern shore, that would be for -
That would be for negro places too as a rule, see, you know. It wasn't many bands playing in the white places then particular in that part of the country.

Do you think that the jazz orchestras that you were working with that were home based in Philadelphia are playing strictly for black audiences, at least in the Philadelphia area, and primarily anywhere they went during this period, 1918, is 'cause this music was so new and really the only people who really appreciated it -
were the black people who knew about it already.
